extracted.intended_audience: general US news readers and media/communications observers interested in broadcast decisions, free speech, and late-night television
extracted.subtask_description: News reporting about a broadcaster/station preempting a late-night comedy program after controversial remarks by the host, covering industry, regulatory, union, and political reactions. Focus is on the standards and arguments used to justify or oppose preemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensiveness / Insensitivity as grounds for action
rubrics_metrics.description: "Mr. Kimmel's comments about the death of Mr. Kirk are offensive and insensitive at a critical time in our national political discourse," (Nexstar) — comments judged offensive/insensitive are cited as justification for preemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an evaluative standard for whether programming should continue to be broadcast. Example: remarks about a killing characterized as "offensive and insensitive" prompted indefinite preemption. Anti-pattern: making remarks that appear to celebrate, trivialize, or exploit a violent death during a heightened political moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflecting the spectrum of local community opinions/values
rubrics_metrics.description: Nexstar: Kimmel's comments "do not reflect the spectrum of opinions, views, or values of the local communities in which we are located."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcasters evaluate programming against perceived community norms and values; lack of alignment can justify withholding content. Guidance implies local affiliates weigh community standards when deciding what to air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serving the public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Nexstar: "Continuing to give Mr. Kimmel a broadcast platform in the communities we serve is simply not in the public interest at the current time."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stations may cite the public-interest standard as a reason to preempt content. This interacts with regulatory language (see FCC). When invoking public interest, owners argue broadcasting decisions should promote community welfare and constructive dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upholding standards expected of a national broadcast platform (remedial preconditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sinclair: will not return the show "until we are confident that appropriate steps have been taken to uphold the standards expected of a national broadcast platform."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcast resumption may be conditioned on demonstrable remedial actions by talent/networks. Examples of requested steps (see separate metric) include apologies and donations. Broadcasters assert an obligation to ensure content meets national-platform standards before reinstating it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial actions: apology and meaningful personal donation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sinclair called on Kimmel to apologize to Kirk's family and make a "meaningful personal donation to the Kirk Family and Turning Point USA."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When offensive comments occur, stations may demand specific remediation from talent: public apology, reparative gestures, or financial contributions. These are presented as tangible steps that could satisfy standards for reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: FCC free-speech constraint and 'clear and present danger' limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: FCC fact sheet: the agency is "barred by law from trying to prevent the broadcast of any point of view." "Expressions of views that do not involve a 'clear and present danger of serious, substantive evil' come under the protection of the Constitution."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory constraint: the FCC generally cannot suppress viewpoints; only speech that meets the high threshold of 'clear and present danger' is unprotected. This is a legal boundary that broadcasters and regulators must consider when justifying preemption or suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stations' unilateral right to preempt programming
rubrics_metrics.description: Nexstar and Sinclair unilaterally announced indefinite preemption/stop airing of "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" on their stations over Kimmel's remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners/operators of local stations can independently choose to preempt network-provided programming on their channels. Preemption is an available operational remedy used to remove content from local airwaves immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-union defense of creative speech and opposition to silencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers Guild of America: stands "united in opposition to anyone who uses their power and influence to silence the voices of writers..." SAG-AFTRA: ABC's decision "is the type of suppression and retaliation that endangers everyone's freedoms."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unions representing creative personnel emphasize protection of speech and warn against employer actions that silence writers/performers. Their stance frames disciplinary/preemptive moves as threats to broader free-expression principles and labor protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer discipline and real-world consequences for controversial comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples in the article: MSNBC fired analyst Matthew Dowd after an on-air comment; The Washington Post dismissed a columnist; a U.S. Secret Service agent was put on leave and had clearance revoked for social-media remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates that individuals (analysts, columnists, government employees) can face suspension, firing, or disciplinary action for statements judged unacceptable. Employers and agencies may act to distance themselves from speech perceived as exacerbating political violence or violating conduct policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political and regulatory actors influencing or responding to broadcast decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Political figures (former President Trump, Senate Minority Leader Schumer) and FCC leadership commented — Trump celebrated cancellation, Schumer urged protection of free speech and legal action, FCC Chair Brendan Carr praised Nexstar and suggested there's a "path forward for suspension."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcasting controversies attract political commentary and potential legal/regulatory responses. Public officials may call for court challenges or regulatory remedies; FCC officials may signal options even as legal limits exist. Such pressure can shape broadcaster choices and public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business and regulatory context shaping programming decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Nexstar "owns and operates more than 200 stations" and "has a deal pending to purchase Tegna... and needs the Federal Communications Commission to approve it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate strategy and pending regulatory approvals can influence station behavior toward programming decisions. Ownership scale, market footprint, and regulatory objectives are contextual factors stations cite or consider when exercising preemption or public-interest claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational messaging to staff about avoiding exacerbation of politically motivated attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Secret Service Director memo: "The men and women of the Secret Service must be focused on being the solution, not adding to the problem."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations, particularly those involved in security or public service, issue internal guidance discouraging public commentary that could exacerbate political violence. This functions as an internal standard for employee public speech.
